items.title: P less than 0.05 doesn't mean a result is true — or even probably true
items.claim: A study finds an effect with p = 0.04. Headlines say 'statistically significant'. The reader assumes the effect is real. In fact, in some scientific fields, more than half of 'p < 0.05' findings fail to replicate.

options.text: The probability the effect is real is 96%

The probability of seeing data at least this extreme IF the null hypothesis is true is 4%. Says nothing directly about the probability the effect is real, which requires Bayesian reasoning with priors
The result is wrong 4% of the time
P-values measure the size of effects

items.reveal_title: P-value misinterpretation and the replication crisis
items.reveal:
P-value definition: P(data at least as extreme as observed | null hypothesis true).

Common misinterpretations:
1. P is the probability the null is true (no).
2. (1 - p) is the probability the effect is real (no).
3. P measures effect size (no — small effects in large studies can have tiny p).
4. P < 0.05 means 'real effect' (no — depends on prior plausibility and study design).

Replication crisis (2010s): many influential findings in psychology, biomedicine, economics fail to replicate.
- Open Science Collaboration (2015) attempted to replicate 100 psychology studies. ~36% of replications succeeded (vs ~97% of original studies reporting significance).
- Reproducibility Project: Cancer Biology (2021) attempted 23 cancer findings; only 25% of effects were as strong in replication.
- Many famous psychology results (ego depletion, power posing, money priming) have not replicated.

Causes:
- P-hacking (running many tests, reporting only significant ones).
- Publication bias (significant findings published; null results filed away).
- Small samples + multiple testing.
- Garden of forking paths (each analytic choice creates uncounted tests).
- Underpowered studies (true effects mixed with noise; significant results when found are overestimates).

Reforms: preregistration, registered reports, focus on effect sizes and confidence intervals, replication studies, statistical training reform, banishing the 0.05 threshold (some journals).

Bayesian alternatives: P(hypothesis | data) directly. Requires explicit priors but gives more interpretable answers.

The ASA's 2016 statement on p-values: don't use 'p < 0.05' as the sole basis for conclusions. Distance is being made from this old standard.
items.why: P-values look like simple measures of certainty. They aren't. Misinterpreting them has contributed to a massive scientific replication crisis. Understanding what p-values do and don't say is essential to reading research.

items.title: London to Tokyo flights cross Siberia — not because Russia is convenient
items.claim: On a flat map, the shortest path between London and Tokyo looks like a horizontal line through Central Asia. The ACTUAL shortest path on Earth's surface arcs north over Siberia. That's the great-circle route.
items.prompt: Why is the great-circle route shortest?

options.text: Any geodesic (shortest path) on a sphere is part of a great circle — a circle whose plane passes through the sphere's centre. Latitude lines (except the equator) are NOT great circles, so flying along a latitude isn't optimal

items.reveal:
A geodesic is the shortest path between two points on a surface. On a flat plane, geodesics are straight lines. On a sphere, geodesics are arcs of great circles — circles whose centre coincides with the sphere's centre.

All meridians (longitude lines, including the prime meridian and date line) are great circles. The equator is a great circle. Lines of latitude EXCEPT the equator are NOT great circles — they're small circles whose plane does not pass through Earth's centre.

London-Tokyo: separated by ~9600 km along the great-circle route, ~12000 km if you fly along the line of latitude (~50°N).

Map projections distort geodesics:
- Mercator projection (Gerardus Mercator, 1569): preserves angles (conformal), shows rhumb lines as straight, but distorts areas and great-circle paths.
- Gnomonic projection: shows great circles as straight lines, but is unsuitable as a navigational chart.
- Robinson, Mollweide: balance distortions in different ways.

Airlines plan routes along great circles, adjusted for winds (jetstream eastbound from US to Europe saves an hour). 'Polar' routes from North America to East Asia routinely cross the Arctic.

In general relativity, geodesics on curved spacetime trace the paths of free-falling objects — gravity IS geodesic motion through curved spacetime.
items.why: Maps lie about distances. Modern navigation requires understanding that the shortest path on a sphere is curved on a flat map. The intuition fails everywhere except locally.

items.title: The cubic formula forced mathematicians to take imaginary numbers seriously
items.claim: Cardano's 1545 formula for cubic equations works perfectly — but its intermediate steps require taking square roots of negative numbers, even when the final answer is a real number. The formula computes real answers via imaginary intermediates.
items.prompt: Why do imaginaries appear in real-answer cubics?

options.text: For cubics with three real roots, Cardano's formula expresses each root as a sum of two cube roots that individually are complex numbers; the imaginary parts cancel in the sum, but cannot be avoided algebraically — this is the 'casus irreducibilis'
Imaginary numbers can be avoided with smarter algebra
Cubics with real roots are computed without complex numbers

items.reveal_title: Casus irreducibilis and the unavoidability of complex numbers
items.reveal:
Cardano's formula for x^3 + px + q = 0:
x = cube root of (-q/2 + sqrt(q^2/4 + p^3/27)) + cube root of (-q/2 - sqrt(q^2/4 + p^3/27)).

When all three roots are real, q^2/4 + p^3/27 is NEGATIVE — so you must take square roots of negatives. The cube roots are complex; their sum is real.

Example: x^3 - 15x - 4 = 0 has solutions x = 4, x = -2 plus or minus sqrt(3). All real.

Cardano's formula gives:
x = cube root of (2 + 11i) + cube root of (2 - 11i)

It's verifiable that 2 + 11i = (2 + i)^3 and 2 - 11i = (2 - i)^3. So x = (2 + i) + (2 - i) = 4. Real answer, computed through imaginary intermediates.

This is called casus irreducibilis (Cardano's term). For three real roots, there is no trigonometric-free, complex-number-free formula. The need for complex numbers is essential, not an avoidable trick.

This forced 16th-17th century mathematicians to take the 'sophistic quantities' seriously. The cubic was the gateway that pushed complex numbers from curiosity into necessity. They would only become geometrically intuitive with Wessel/Argand/Gauss in the 1790s-1830s — but their usefulness was inescapable from 1545 onward.

The quartic was solved by Cardano's student Ferrari (also published in Ars Magna). The quintic, as Galois and Abel showed centuries later, cannot be solved by radicals at all.
items.why: Real-world problems suggest only real numbers. The algebra of cubics shows that even the simplest real-coefficient real-root polynomials force complex arithmetic in their solution. Imaginaries aren't optional.
